questions.text: How long have you been coughing up blood, and how would you describe the amount — streaks only, or frank blood?
questions.purpose: Characterise onset and volume; massive haemoptysis (>200 mL/24 h) requires immediate escalation
options: Frank red blood, small volume (<50 mL/episode)
Frank red blood, large volume (>50 mL/episode)

questions.text: Are you currently coughing up large amounts of blood (more than a few tablespoons)?
questions.purpose: Massive haemoptysis is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate escalation

questions.text: Do you have a history of significant smoking (more than 10 pack-years) or exposure to asbestos or radon?
questions.purpose: Smoking and asbestos are major risk factors for lung malignancy in the context of haemoptysis

questions.text: Have you experienced significant unintentional weight loss, fatigue, or decreased appetite over the past few months?
questions.purpose: Constitutional symptoms alongside haemoptysis increase likelihood of lung malignancy

questions.text: Do you have a persistent new cough or a change in your usual cough pattern lasting more than 3 weeks?
questions.purpose: Persistent cough change is a key lung cancer symptom alongside haemoptysis

questions.text: Have you had any recent chest infections, confirmed tuberculosis exposure, or known bronchiectasis?
questions.purpose: Identify common benign causes of haemoptysis that can lower oncology suspicion

questions.text: Have you noticed hoarseness of voice, difficulty swallowing, or new facial swelling?
questions.purpose: Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve) and SVC obstruction signs suggest mediastinal involvement
